name: Good sunglasses

lead: Sunglasses are tinted or polarized eyewear that reduces glare and ultraviolet exposure. Frame shape also changes how the face reads.
In style advice they are used to balance facial proportions and add polish. The visual effect is immediate, though no specific scholarly literature was reviewed here.

paras: Tinted lenses cut visible light and UV, while frame shape, width and bridge alter perceived proportions.
Poorly rated lenses can let UV in; guidance is to check for UV400 or equivalent labeling. Frames that fit badly are uncomfortable. The effect lasts only while worn.

lead: Sunglasses are tinted or darkened eyewear designed mainly to reduce glare and protect the eyes from bright light, including ultraviolet radiation.[1] They have also been a popular fashion accessory since the 1930s.[1] In appearance advice, a well-chosen pair is said to change how the face reads, with frame shape and width used to balance facial proportions, and the wiki's summary describes frames as reframing proportions.

The protective function is supported by ophthalmic and dermatological guidance, while the cosmetic claim about face shape is a style convention for which no controlled study was found. The American Optometric Association is cited by Wikipedia as recommending UV-blocking sunglasses whenever a person is in sunlight.[1]
infobox: ISO 12312 (general-use sunglasses, first published 2013, new edition 2022) [1]
UV400 (blocks about 99% or more of UVA and UVB up to 400 nm) [1]
Regulated by the FDA; ANSI Z80.3 transmittance categories [1]

paras: Frames are generally made of plastic, nylon, metal or metal alloys. Nylon is common in sport because it is light and flexible, while metal frames are more rigid. Nose-bridge height is chosen to fit the wearer's nose, and lens colours such as grey and green are described as neutral because they preserve colour, with brown giving more contrast.[1]

Wikipedia lists well-known fashion shapes with their origins: the aviator, introduced by Bausch & Lomb in 1936 for US military aviators; the browline, adapted into sunglasses in the 1980s; the Ray-Ban Wayfarer, introduced in 1952; wrap-arounds, first made in the 1960s; oversized frames; teashades; and shutter shades. It also describes gradient and clip-on lenses.[1]

Wikipedia traces precursors to Inuit snow goggles with narrow slits, used since at least the thirteenth century, and to smoky quartz panes used in China in the twelfth century or earlier, with accounts that Chinese judges wore them to conceal expressions.[1] Jean-Marie-Theodore Fieuzal argued for UV protection with yellow-tinted glasses in the nineteenth century, and Rodenstock produced possibly the first sunglasses aimed at UV in 1899. Crookes lenses containing cerium were introduced in 1913.[1]

Sunglasses spread widely in the 1920s among film stars. Sam Foster began selling inexpensive celluloid sunglasses under the Foster Grant name in Atlantic City in 1929, and by 1938 Life magazine described them as a city-street fad.[1]

Tinted lenses lower visible-light transmission, and UV-filtering coatings or materials reduce ultraviolet exposure. Polarised lenses reduce glare reflected from surfaces such as water and road.[1] Wikipedia adds that eye-protective guidance recommends lenses that filter 99% or more of UVA and UVB, often labelled UV400, and that the only way to assess protection is to measure the lenses; standards allow general classification.[1]

Wikipedia also notes that dark lenses without UV filtering can be more harmful than none because the pupil dilates and lets in more UV radiation.[1] Frame fit matters for stray light: lenses should be close enough to the face that little light enters from the sides, without touching the eyelashes.[1]

Photoprotection reviews list sunglasses among physical measures, alongside clothing, hats and sunscreen, against ultraviolet exposure.[2][3] UV radiation is described in a 2024 review as the main cause of photoageing, photoimmunosuppression and photocarcinogenesis.[3] Sunglasses protect the eyes and skin around them, though most of the cited evidence addresses sun protection in general rather than eyewear alone.

Wikipedia reports that sunglasses can hide eye contact and emotions, which can be seen as desirable or intimidating, and that many professional poker players wear them for this reason.[1] The claim that particular frame shapes make a face look more balanced has not been studied in the sources reviewed.

Sunglasses can improve driving safety by reducing glare but may be too dark for driving if poorly chosen, and photochromic lenses react slowly behind car windscreens that filter UV.[1] Polarised lenses can interfere with aircraft windscreens and some instrument displays.[1] Frames that fit poorly can be uncomfortable. Labelling varies by region; European EN 1836 uses categories without a UV400 rating, while the United States uses ANSI Z80.3.[1]

In style communities, sunglasses are discussed as an inexpensive accessory that can hide eye area features, adjust apparent face width and add polish. Proponents recommend matching frame shape to face shape in order to balance proportions. These ideas come from style advice and have not been tested in controlled studies.

Reference descriptions list features to compare: a UV400 or equivalent standard label, lens tint and polarisation, frame material, nose-bridge fit, and snug fit to the face to limit stray light.[1] The same source says protection can only be confirmed by measuring lenses, so labels indicating conformity with a named standard are the usual indicator.[1]

No studies found that test sunglasses for facial appearance or perceived attractiveness. Related research on sunglasses as sun protection includes a Turkish survey of 17,769 university students in which 60% reported using sunglasses, behind sunscreen at 64%,[4] and a randomised trial of sunglasses for conjunctival symptoms of seasonal rhinitis.[5] A 2026 randomised trial in the Journal of Affective Disorders tested blue-blocking glasses for mania, which concerns a different kind of eyewear and condition.[6] These studies address protection and health outcomes rather than appearance.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sunglasses are discussed as a cheap accessory that hides or reframes the eye area and midface, rather than mainly for eye protection. [7][8][9]

claims.claim: Sunglasses are a cheap substitute for eye-area surgery and hide flaws such as bad canthal tilt or recessed orbitals.
Specific frame shapes balance facial proportions depending on face shape.
People with long midfaces, bug eyes or wide noses look noticeably better in sunglasses.

timeline.event: Inuit snow goggles with narrow slits are in use, per Wikipedia.[1]
